list.listitem: Clinical presentation generally consists of CNS depression, drowsiness, slurred speech, nystagmus, coma, respiratory depression, and hypotension. C
Address the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation). Do not give ipecac or activated charcoal without recommendation from a poison center or emergency department. C

Flumazenil, 0.2 mg IV bolus over 30 seconds with repeat doses of 0.3 to 0.5 mg in 30-second increments, will reverse the sedation and respiratory depression associated with benzodiazepine toxicity but should not be used in patients with suspected seizure disorder or who also have taken tricyclic antidepressants. A

Using 2001 to 2007 Missouri Hospital Discharge Data for Kansas City, Missouri, benzodiazepine poisoning occurred in 0.04% of emergency department visits (562/1,317,566); white race and ages 30 to 49 years were identified risk factors.

Among 1,700 trauma victims admitted to one hospital, 20% were on prescription narcotics and/or benzodiazepines at the time of admission. Both total and ICU length of stay and were significantly longer, by over 1 day, for these patients.
In a study of 895 Swedish drivers killed in road-traffic crashes, 7.6% had blood levels of psychoactive prescription drugs, primarily benzodiazepines, z-hypnotics and tramadol.

In a British Columbia study of nursing home admissions over a 10-year period, 44% of the 10,900 patients started on a psychotropic medication were started on a benzodiazepine. Users of benzodiazepines had a higher risk of death than users of atypical antipsychotics (RR 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04-1.58).
Alprazolam and diazepam were among the top 10 drug drugs involved in drug overdose deaths in the United States from 2010 through 2014.

Benzodiazepine use was estimated at 5.2% of US adults aged 18 to 80 years based on a prescription database that includes approximately 60% of all retail pharmacies in the United States. Use increased with increasing age and was twice as prevalent in women as men.

Among 356 young adults in the US, ages 18 to 29 years, who participated in the electronic dance music culture in Miami, prevalence of BZD-related problems was 12.6% for benzodiazepine dependence and 21.1% for abuse.
Among users of opioids identified in an administrative health claims database, concomitant use of a benzodiazepine increased from 9% in 2001 to 17% in 2013.

In keeping with the doubling of the number of Medicare beneficiaries between 1991 and 2009, prescriptions for benzodiazepines among Medicaid beneficiaries increased from 8.0 million in 1991 to 17.1 million in 2009. Expenditures rose from $131.6 million to $171.1 million over the same time period, likely due to availability of generics.
In a French database study, use of benzodiazepine hypnotics increased the risk of being responsible for an injury-related traffic accident (OR 1.39; 95% CI, 1.08-1.79).

In a Finish national database study, benzodiazepine use was associated with increased mortality among patients with schizophrenia (HR 1.91; 95% CI, 1.13-3.22), including both suicidal and nonsuicidal deaths. Benzodiazepine use was also associated with increased mortality among patients starting long-term oxygen therapy for COPD, and among patients who received opioids.
Use of benzodiazepines are associated with an increased risk of attempting or completing suicide.
Unlike morphine, postoperative use of benzodiazepines were associated with an increased risk of delirium in patients undergoing total joint arthroplasty.
Patients with benzodiazepine poisoning have a 5.33-fold increased risk of developing acute pancreatitis within 1 month compared to control patients.
There is also an association between benzodiazepine use and epilepsy (adjusted OR 2.02; 95% CI, 1.68-2.42) that demonstrates a dose-response relationship.

Long-term use of clonazepam (Hazard Ratio 1.15; 95% CI, 1.09-1.22) was associated with a higher risk for brain, colorectal and lung cancers based on a case-control study using 12 years from Taiwan National Health Insurance database. There was no increased cancer risk observed with use of diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, medazepam, nitrazepam, or oxazepam.
Conazepam for neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia in adults has insufficient evidence for its use
In a meta-analysis from 2023, for low back pain, the evidence supporting benzodiazepine or non-benzodiazepine “muscle relaxants” is of low certainty and they are not recommended.

In a cohort study of 2,802 Canadian individuals who injected drugs and were followed for a median of 67 months, benzodiazepine use was independently associated with increased all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 1.86; 95% CI, 1.38-2.51) and had a higher risk for mortality than all other identified substances of abuse; 527 (18.8%) died.

Concomitant use of benzodiazepines with opioids increases risk of ED visit or inpatient admission for opioid overdose (adjusted OR 2.14, 95% CI, 2.05-2.24). In a cohort of 50 people using injected drugs who reported a nonfatal overdose, poly drug use was common and benzodiazepines were implicated in just over half of the overdoses.
It is unclear if benzodiazepines improve outcomes for people with catatonia secondary to schizophrenia or similar serious mental illness.
Benzodiazepine binding at the γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) A receptor results in therapeutic effects, such as sedation, muscle relaxation, anxiolysis, and anticonvulsant effects.
Stimulation of GABA receptors in the peripheral nervous system may result in decreased cardiac contractility, vasodilation, and enhanced perfusion.

Psychomotor slowing may also result from benzodiazepine administration; psychomotor symptoms include drowsiness, poor concentration, ataxia, dysarthria, motor incoordination, diplopia, muscle weakness, vertigo, and mental confusion.

Use of a screening tool (e.g., Screening Tool of Older Person's potentially inappropriate Prescriptions/Screening Tool to Alert doctors to the Right, ie appropriate, indicated Treatment [STOPP-START] criteria or the Australian criteria) can be used to detect potentially inappropriate drug prescriptions in older people on admission to a nursing home. In one cross-sectional study of 100 patients, these tools identified at least 1 potentially inappropriate prescription in 79% to 95%. Benzodiazepines were among the most frequent potentially inappropriate drugs prescribed.

Prescription monitoring programs intended to address benzodiazepine over-prescription were found to reduce benzodiazepine prescribing, but the decline was not consistent across population groups; marginalized and vulnerable populations (e.g., those with chronic mental health disorders) appeared to be disproportionately affected.

Implementing a prior-authorization pharmacy consult to reduce opioid/benzodiazepine co-prescribing as part of an Opioid Safety Initiative in a single VA center resulted in a 34.6% reduction in co-prescribed opioids and benzodiazepines and decreased the total number of overdose-related events.

A brief intervention for ED patients identified as persons with substance use disorders was not effective in reducing drug use and misuse or increase treatment utilization more than the control condition over a 3-month period.

The clinical presentation of patients intoxicated with benzodiazepines is similar to that of individuals intoxicated with alcohol. It generally consists of CNS depression, drowsiness, slurred speech, nystagmus, coma, respiratory depression, and hypotension.

Flubromazolam is a new designer drug that is a long-lasting psychoactive drug of the benzodiazepine class. Recreational use may be a cause of prolonged, severe intoxication associated with coma, hypotension, and rhabdomyolysis.
Misuse of benzodiazepines is more common in older patients and those who are physically or mentally vulnerable, especially those with insomnia or who use other psychotropic medications.

Obtain history and objective proof, if possible, of the specific agent ingested; dose; time of ingestion; and presence or absence of concomitant ingestion of other CNS or respiratory depressants, especially tricyclic antidepressants.

The Severity of Dependence Scale has high diagnostic utility for benzodiazepine dependence with a score >6 identifying dependence with a specificity of 94.2%, a sensitivity of 97.9%, and area under the curve of 0.991. A Chinese version was found to be slightly less effective (specificity of 85.7%, a sensitivity of 80.5%, and the area under the curve 0.779).
Interview family, friends, local pharmacies, and/or treating physicians regarding the length of benzodiazepine treatment.
Review prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) for prescribed benzodiazepines.
Patients suspected of benzodiazepine poisoning should have all of their vital signs checked, as well as undergo a full mental status and neurologic examination.

Most often, urine screening is performed to confirm the presence of benzodiazepines. A recently developed rapid detection method using ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry may improve benzodiazepine urine screening.
Quantitative screening of the blood by gas chromatography is the most efficient means of detection, but quantitative results often do not change treatment choices.
Hair can also be used to detect drugs of misuse including benzodiazepines. In one study, hair analysis was more sensitive than maternal interview in detecting drug use during pregnancy.

An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (LUCIO-Direct ELISA kit) had a sensitivity of 96% for benzodiazepines. In a German study, relative sensitivities and specificities were higher for ELISA than for cloned enzyme donor immunoassays for urine drug screening (including detection of benzodiazepines).
If benzodiazepines are used alone, breath and blood alcohol levels should be zero.

Flumazenil administration can differentiate between patients with benzodiazepine-induced coma (prolonged wakefulness after 1 mg of flumazenil) and patients with nonbenzodiazepine-induced coma (short-lived wakefulness), as well as coma due to other causes (no effect after 2.5 mg of flumazenil).
In the presence of respiratory depression, obtain arterial blood gas value and a chest x-ray.

In situations with acute drug overdose, admission ECG can be helpful for predicting adverse cardiovascular events. One study found QT correction >500 ms to be the highest risk feature for an adverse event; the most common drug exposures in this study were benzodiazepines, opioids, and acetaminophen.
Address the ABCs.
Do not give ipecac or activated charcoal without recommendation from a poison center or ED. C

Flumazenil, a specific benzodiazepine antagonist, reverses sedation and respiratory depression associated with benzodiazepine toxicity. The dosage is 2 mL (0.2 mg) IV bolus over 30 seconds. If there is no response, give 0.3 to 0.5 mg (3-5 mL) doses in 30-second increments. Most patients respond to doses between 0.2 and 1.0 mg.
IV flumazenil will reach peak serum levels within minutes and has a half-life of 41 to 79 minutes.
The establishment and maintenance of upper airway patency, oxygenation, and ventilatory support should be done prior to the administration of flumazenil.

Flumazenil can quickly induce benzodiazepine withdrawal symptoms, especially in patients who are physically dependent. Flumazenil should also be administered with caution in patients with a history of seizure disorders, hemodynamic instability, electrocardiogram signs of tricyclic overdose, or evidence of ingestion of high doses of a tricyclic antidepressant. Adverse events associated with flumazenil include agitation and gastrointestinal symptoms and serious adverse events, occurring in 2.4% in one meta-analysis, include supraventricular arrhythmia and convulsions.

Aminophylline may be a second-line agent for cases for which flumazenil is contraindicated as one RCT demonstrated it decreased time to full awakening in those who received aminophylline following in intentional benzodiazepine poisoning compared to placebo (72 min vs. 881 min).
Manage benzodiazepine withdrawal by using either a slow taper of original benzodiazepine or by switching the patient to a benzodiazepine with a longer half-life (chlordiazepoxide or clonazepam).
If the toxicity was due to suicide attempt or suspected suicide attempt, the patient should be referred to a psychiatrist for a full psychiatric evaluation.

In a RCT of patients with combined post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and substance use disorder (including benzodiazepines), a combination of exposure therapy (a cognitive-behavioral therapy that exposes patients to memories of past trauma) and treatment for substance use disorder was more effective than substance use disorder treatment alone for reducing PTSD scores; no differences were seen, however, in severity of substance use, depression, anxiety, or suicide attempts.

Combined with weekly CBT-I, an RCT showed that a masked tapering of a nightly benzodiazepine hypnotic is significantly more effective than when patients doing their own taper. Mask tapering involves a pharmacist preparing identical capsules containing progressively lower doses of the benzodiazepine for each week, and therapy aimed at promoting the placebo effect of medication tapering by shaping patient expectations.
Mortality is very rare for patients who have solely ingested a benzodiazepine, with aspiration being the main complication that could lead to death.
Mortality increases with concomitant alcohol or other CNS depressants, with ingestion of short-acting agents (triazolam), and in elderly patients.
There is a black box warning for concomitant benzodiazepine and opioid ingestion due to increased risk of respiratory depression.
Flumazenil has been shown to improve the mortality rate by lowering the need for mechanical ventilation and facilitating extubation.

Infants with known exposure to opioids and benzodiazepines in utero should be observed in the hospital for 4 to 7 days, preferably with a family-based intervention like Eat, Sleep, Console. These drugs generally clear in 1 to 3 days after birth.

Signs of withdrawal in newborns from diazepam include hypotonia, poor suck, hypothermia, apnea, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, tremors, vomiting, hyperactivity, and tachypnea. Onset of signs is hours to weeks after birth and duration can be up to 8 months.
A hospital-based protocol for evaluation and management, including use of an abstinence assessment tool, should be developed and used.

Drug treatment (opioids [tincture of opium, neonatal morphine solution, methadone, and paregoric], barbiturates [phenobarbital], benzodiazepines [diazepam, lorazepam], clonidine, and phenothiazines [chlorpromazine]) are used to relieve moderate to severe signs of neonatal abstinence syndrome. The optimal agent is not known and a discussion of treatment trials and reviews and weaning protocols can be found in the cited reference. Treatment of drug withdrawal may not alter long-term outcomes.
Early follow-up is also encouraged to reinforce education on late withdrawal signs.

Use of IV midazolam infusion as a sedative in neonates is of uncertain effectiveness and increased ICU duration of stay and, in one small study increased adverse neurological events at 28 days compared to morphine.

Older patients may be more vulnerable to benzodiazepine toxicity; in one study of 387 consecutive patients presenting to the hospital with benzodiazepine toxicity, the incidence of coma, respiratory failure and aspiration pneumonia was significantly higher, and the length of hospital stay significantly longer, in patients >65 years compared to younger patients.
